problems.title: A fixed \(0.2\) expert cap disagrees with Eq. (5) and can make class normalization undefined
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, Eq. (5), PDF pp. 6–7; released expert-weight cap and class-normalization implementation.
claim: Paraphrase preserving the relevant domain: Section 3.4, pp. 6–7, assigns newly introduced experts weight \(\alpha\), increases it by \(\beta\) per subsequent task, and caps each non-base weight at \(1/K\). Equation (5) gives, for active experts,
analysis: For \(K=3\), the stated saturated expert weights are \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\), but a fixed \(0.2\) cap gives \((0.6,0.2,0.2)\). For \(K=6\), five non-base weights of \(0.2\) leave base weight zero, so a class eligible only for the base expert encounters normalization \(0/0\). These permitted settings show a local cap mismatch, not failure of every default run.

The explicit legal schedule uses \(K=6\), initial weight \(0.10\), increment \(0.05\), and \(40\) base classes followed by \(20\) tasks of \(3\) classes. At task \(7\), the five non-base weights reach \(0.2\), making the base residual zero. Under the paper cap \(1/6\), the residual is at least \(1/6\). The default \(K=5\) cap agrees with the formula.
result: The general expert-count release can become undefined, but the main five-expert configuration passes this specific cap control.
repair: Use cap \(1/K\), with initial weights also in \([0,1/K]\) and nonnegative increments. At most \(K-1\) non-base weights then leave residual at least \(1/K>0\), preserving positive class denominators through the always-eligible base expert.
problems.impact_rationale: The general expert-count release can become undefined, but the main five-expert configuration passes this specific cap control.

problems.title: The released shared, frozen ResNet prefix can change during later-expert training
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p. 5; Section 4.1, PDF p. 8; Appendix C.3 and Table 9, PDF pp. 23–24; released clover.py sharing loop.
claim: Section 3.2, PDF p. 5, states a shared encoder frozen after the first task. Section 4.1 and Appendix C.3, PDF pp. 8 and \(23\)–\(24\), describe sharing its first layers. Released clover.py, lines 74–81 and \(211\)–\(229\), chooses parameter names \(\texttt{conv1\_starting}\) and \(\texttt{bn1\_starting}\), aliases selected parameters and disables their gradients. The actual network stem in resnet_linear_turbo.py is named \(\texttt{conv1}\) and \(\texttt{bn1}\). Each training epoch also calls model.train().
analysis: The requested stem names do not match the actual \(\texttt{conv1}\) and \(\texttt{bn1}\) parameters, leaving those parameters trainable. Even corrected parameter aliases omit BatchNorm running-mean and variance buffers, which model.train() updates. Freezing gradients therefore does not preserve the claimed single shared frozen encoder function.
result: Stem-name mismatch and mutable BatchNorm state defeat the claimed released prefix invariant; corrected benchmark accuracy and historical checkout correspondence remain unknown.
repair: Share the actual prefix modules, freeze their parameters, and restore the frozen BatchNorm modules to evaluation mode after each general training-mode call. Parameter flags alone do not freeze buffers.
problems.impact_rationale: Stem-name mismatch and mutable BatchNorm state defeat the claimed released prefix invariant; corrected benchmark accuracy and historical checkout correspondence remain unknown.
problems.existing_correction_status: A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

impact_rationale: Both findings persist in current released paths, with a passing default cap control and no retrained accuracy comparison. The demonstrated scope is local implementation, so the paper remains Minor.
